summary: Describes several Rate Adaptive Shapers for Differentiated Services that can be used with the single rate and two rate Three Color Markers from RFC 2697 and RFC 2698.

eli5.summary: This smooths out a flow of data so it fits the rate a network promised, adjusting as needed.

questions: traffic shaping with three color marker
how to improve tcp in diffserv
subtitle: Techniques to improve TCP performance in DiffServ networks by reducing traffic burstiness

tldr.problem: Token bucket-based traffic markers like the Three Color Marker (TCM) can cause TCP to behave poorly because they mark many packets when traffic arrives in bursts, reducing the fraction of unmarked packets and lowering application throughput.
tldr.mechanism: A Rate Adaptive Shaper (RAS) places a FIFO queue upstream of the TCM and controls its output rate based on the estimated average incoming traffic rate and the queue occupancy. This reduces burstiness and increases the percentage of packets marked green by the TCM.
tldr.outcome: TCP performance improves when a RAS is placed at the network edge, particularly when handling a small number of TCP connections. Two variants (single-rate and two-rate) and enhanced green variants are described.

today: RFC 2963 is Informational and describes techniques for improving TCP goodput in DiffServ networks that use Three Color Markers. The RFC applies at the network edge and has been useful in research and operational settings where TCM-based QoS is deployed.

sections.title: TCP and Traffic Marking in DiffServ
sections.content:
DiffServ networks use markers like the single-rate Three Color Marker (srTCM, RFC 2697) and two-rate Three Color Marker (trTCM, RFC 2698) to classify traffic into marked and unmarked packets, where marked packets receive a higher drop probability. These markers are based on token buckets: they allow a Committed Information Rate (CIR) of unmarked traffic and a Peak Information Rate (PIR) for two-rate markers, with burst allowances.

The problem arises with TCP: when traffic arrives in bursts, the TCM marks many packets at once, forcing TCP to back off aggressively. This reduces goodput (the application-layer throughput) even though the network has capacity. Simulations have shown that increasing burst sizes only shifts the problem to network engineering (more buffering needed), whereas shaping the traffic before the TCM can reduce burstiness and improve TCP performance without requiring larger buffers.
sections.eli5: A traffic marker checks if your data is coming too fast, and if it is, it marks packets as less important so the network will drop them first. But when data arrives in bursts, the marker gets confused and marks too many packets at once, making the application slow down.

sections.title: Rate Adaptive Shaper Architecture
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a Rate Adaptive Shaper that sits upstream of the TCM. It consists of a tail-drop FIFO queue that is emptied at a variable rate. Unlike classical token-bucket shapers that discard packets to enforce a rate, the RAS avoids discarding: it buffers packets and adjusts the output rate to prevent loss and excessive delay.

The shaping rate is computed as the maximum of two factors: the estimated average rate of incoming traffic and a function of the buffer occupancy. When the queue is mostly empty, the shaper sends traffic at the average rate. As queue occupancy rises, the shaper increases its output rate to drain the queue and prevent it from filling completely. This adaptive approach reduces burstiness while maintaining good throughput.
sections.eli5: A shaper is like a water faucet with a queue of buckets. It opens wider when the queue gets long, and lets water out slowly when the queue is short. This smooths out the flow.

sections.title: Single-Rate and Two-Rate Shapers
sections.content:
The RFC specifies two types of shapers: single-rate (srRAS) for use with srTCM, and two-rate (trRAS) for use with trTCM. The srRAS is configured with a Committed Information Rate (CIR), a Maximum Information Rate (MIR), and two buffer thresholds: CIR_th and MIR_th. When buffer occupancy is below CIR_th, the shaper outputs at least the CIR. As occupancy rises above CIR_th, a linear function increases the output rate toward MIR.

The trRAS adds a Peak Information Rate (PIR) and three thresholds. It behaves similarly but with a piecewise linear function that increases from CIR to PIR as occupancy rises from CIR_th to PIR_th, then from PIR to MIR as occupancy rises further. The output rate is always at least the estimated average rate to prevent unnecessary delays.
sections.eli5: There are two shapers: one for simple quality-of-service (marked or unmarked) and one for more complex quality-of-service (committed, peak, or maximum rates). Each one adjusts its speed differently based on how many packets are waiting.

sections.title: Configuration Parameters and Thresholds
sections.content:
The RFC specifies that the Committed Information Rate (CIR) must be configurable and must be specified in bytes per second. For good performance, the CIR should usually match the CIR of the downstream TCM. The Maximum Information Rate (MIR) should typically be set to the output link rate.

The buffer thresholds CIR_th and MIR_th (or CIR_th, PIR_th, MIR_th for two-rate) should be configurable in bytes. Their values typically depend on the Committed Burst Size (CBS) and Peak Burst Size (PBS) of the downstream TCM, though the RFC does not standardize this dependency. The constraint is that the thresholds must be ordered: CIR_th <= MIR_th <= buffer size.
sections.eli5: The shaper needs to know three things: the committed rate (how fast it promises), the maximum rate (how fast the line is), and when to start speeding up (buffer thresholds). These are settings you configure based on your network.

sections.title: Estimated Average Rate and Adaptive Behavior
sections.content:
The shaper computes an Estimated Average Rate (EAR) of incoming traffic. One common approach is an exponential moving average: EARnew = [(1-exp(-T/K))*L/T] + exp(-T/K)*EARold, where L is the size of the arriving packet, T is the time since the previous packet arrived, and K is a constant controlling how quickly the estimate reacts to changes. Other averaging methods are acceptable.

The output rate is set to the maximum of the EAR and a function of buffer occupancy. This ensures that traffic flowing through is processed at its natural rate when the queue is light, but faster when the queue builds up. The RFC notes that real implementations may use an approximation of the specified function rather than the exact formula.
sections.eli5: The shaper watches how fast data is arriving on average and uses that to decide how fast to send it out. It also watches how long the queue is getting and speeds up if it gets too full.

sections.title: Green Shapers and Status
sections.content:
The RFC also describes an enhanced variant called the "green RAS" that couples the shaper with the downstream marker. The green RAS computes when a packet would be marked green by the TCM and releases it at that time if possible, rather than always delaying until the configured shaping rate allows. This gives lower latency for traffic that will be marked green, improving TCP performance further.

RFC 2963 is informational and applies specifically to srTCM and trTCM. The techniques are intended for deployment at network edges, such as in access routers or network adapters. They are particularly useful when a small number of TCP connections are being processed, a common scenario in edge networks. Simulation results in the appendix demonstrate the performance improvements when RAS is combined with TCM for TCP traffic.
sections.eli5: An even better version, the green shaper, talks to the marker downstream to release packets faster if it knows they will be marked as okay. And the whole idea works best when you have just a few TCP connections all arriving at once.
